The Lighthouse Keeper

By: Annalise Lubbe | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
On a rugged stretch of the West Coast, one man keeps the lantern burning. We follow the story of one of South Africa's final lighthouse keepers - as he keeps watch over the sea that has shaped his lif

Unique Selling Point:
Lighthouses stand as timeless symbols of hope, safety, and endurance - their beams cutting through the fog and darkness to guide sailors home. But behind every shining light once stood a keeper: a quiet guardian who ensured the flame never went out.


Summary:
OVERVIEW
Amid crashing waves and coastal winds, Cape Columbine Lighthouse stands as a steadfast beacon.

At 52, Wayne Brown has spent most of his life fulfilling that duty. Born in Paternoster and raised within sight of the tower, Wayne’s bond with the ocean runs deep. His grandfather captained a crayfish vessel; his parents worked on the lighthouse reserve. Mentored by veteran keeper Japie Greeff, Wayne inherited both the tools and the calling to keep the light burning, no matter the weather.

Cape Columbine, built in 1936 and named after a ship wrecked nearby in 1829, remains one of the last manned lighthouses on South Africa’s 3,000-kilometre coastline. Most others have been automated — visited only occasionally by technicians. Yet Wayne remains, faithfully tending the beam that still cuts through fog and darkness to guide sailors safely home.
“Every time a ship passes,” he says, “I know I’ve helped it find safe passage.”

STORY OUTLINE
ACT 1 — INTRODUCTION
We open on a windswept coastline at dawn. Waves crash against the rocks as the revolving light fades into morning. A single figure walks the narrow path to the tower — Wayne Brown. Through reflective narration and natural sound, we meet the man behind the beam: a custodian of history, solitude, and purpose.
ACT 2 — A LIFE BY THE SEA
Through interviews and observational sequences, we trace Wayne’s life story — his childhood in the reserve, the mentorship of Japie Greeff, and the rhythm of his days at Cape Columbine. The film captures his maintenance routines, logbook entries, and quiet rituals that keep the lighthouse alive.
ACT 3 — KEEPING THE LIGHT ALIVE
As automation spreads, Wayne reflects on being among the last of his kind. The tone becomes more introspective: what does it mean to dedicate your life to a duty few now understand? Wayne’s voice anchors the narrative, culminating in his poetic reflection:
“Die vuurtoring is ‘n lig vir die mense wat op die see is... Jy moet liefde hê vir die werk. Jy moet alles kan insit.”
(The lighthouse is a light for those at sea — to show them where the safe path lies. You must have love for the work. You must give it your all.)
The story closes at dusk — the light once again sweeping over the waves, a quiet testament to endurance.

THEMES
Tradition vs. Technology – A human craft fading in the digital age.


Solitude and Purpose – Finding meaning in isolation and service.


Legacy and Heritage – Preserving South Africa’s maritime past.


Faith and Devotion – The lighthouse as both a beacon and a metaphor for steadfastness.



TONE & VISUAL STYLE
The tone is contemplative, poetic, and authentic — rooted in natural sound, minimal narration, and strong visual storytelling.
Visual Style:
Cinematic, slow-paced camera movement with emphasis on texture and light.


A restrained colour palette of muted blues, whites, and greys, reflecting the Atlantic coast’s timeless quality.


Wide aerials juxtaposed with intimate close-ups of Wayne’s hands, the turning lens, and salt-worn metal.


Use of archival photographs and soundscapes (waves, gulls, foghorn) to evoke continuity and nostalgia.


Key Visual Sequences:
The revolving lantern at dusk and dawn.


Wayne performing routine maintenance.


The foghorn echoing across the sea.


Archival stills of lighthouses on the South African coastline.


Expansive views of the Cape Columbine Nature Reserve.



WHY THIS STORY MATTERS
The Lighthouse Keeper is a tribute to the quiet guardians who have watched over South Africa’s shores for generations. As automation replaces human presence, Wayne’s story preserves a piece of national heritage — reminding us that some lights still need a human touch.
This is not just a story about a lighthouse. It is about duty, legacy, and devotion — a deeply human story told through the lens of one man’s enduring relationship with the sea.

DELIVERABLES
Broadcast-ready short documentary insert (8–10 minutes)


Supporting stills of some of the lighthouses on the South African coastline
______________________________________________________________________________________________


Extra Budget Items:
Accommodation for 4 people for one night at the Cape Columbine Rererve self catering units. Traveling cost to Cape Columbine Lighthouse in Tietiesbaai, near Paternoster.
Drone camera x 1 day shoot for aerial visuals

Broadcast format script: The Lighthouse Keeper
Date: 20 November 2025
Duration: 10 minutes 23 seconds

(Wayne Brown) For me, it’s about the people that go to sea every day, and the lighthouse is there to guide them.

(Erin) At the Cape Columbine Lighthouse, near the West Coast fishing village of Paternoster, a lighthouse keeper begins his day.

(Erin) 52-year-old Wayne Brown has spent half his life here.

(Wayne Brown) Every ship, for every boat that pass by, and they make use of the lighthouse, and they pass by and they come back safe, for me, it is something big.

(Erin) Along the coast in the wildest places where the sea's crazy and the fog is always rolling in, you will find a lighthouse, and it takes a very special person to live out here.

(Wayne Brown) Hi.

(Erin) Hello.

(Wayne Brown) Hi. My name is Wayne. I’m glad to show you how the lighthouse works. A little bit of the history I want to explain to you.

(Erin) Please, let’s go.

(Wayne Brown) Let’s come inside.

(Erin) Thank you.

(Wayne Brown) You’re more than welcome.

Erin: Wayne has a deep connection to the lighthouse. He grew up in Paternoster, where his parents worked on the lighthouse reserve and his grandfather captained a crayfish vessel.

(Wayne Brown) My stepfather was the general worker here. Every time I came from school I was very fascinating and I’d come with him, look what he’s doing. And I told myself, when I finish high school, I want to become a lighthouse keeper.

(Erin) After twice missing out, Wayne eventually graduated from general worker to lighthouse keeper when his predecessor and mentor, Japie Greeff, retired.

(Wayne Brown) I go down on my knees and I pray to God and I say: “God, thank you very much. Thank you very much for making my dream come true today.”

(Erin) From its position in a nature reserve, Cape Columbine lighthouse has watched over the coast since 1936. Back then, much of the equipment was operated by hand, including the towering foghorn, which produced its deep sound from compressed air stored in tanks being released through valves.

(Wayne Brown) This is the compressor room, this is the old foghorn, it was used in the old days.

(Erin) Like every lighthouse, this one comes with its fair share of steps.

(Erin) Ooh, it’s a lot of steps Wayne.

(Wayne Brown) Yah you must be tired, you must be fit to do it.

(Erin) Yeah, I’m getting my workout.

(Wayne Brown) This is the thing I want to show you. As soon as this tank got full of compressed air, they open this two valves here and the other one here, and the air goes to those two pipes and it makes a sound like: “Boo”. Then it stop. After a minute: “Boo”. We have foggy weather. The ships can’t see the light. That’s why the foghorn must be on.

(Erin) In 1995, the old foghorn fell silent — replaced by a modern electric system capable of reaching kilometers out to sea.

(Erin) But, as technology advanced, the ocean remained as unpredictable as ever.

(Wayne Brown) “Port Control, Port Control, Port Control.This is Cape Columbine lighthouse. This is Cape Columbine lighthouse.”

(Erin) Wayne remembers a stormy night in June 2013 when a fishing boat fought desperately to find its way home.

(Wayne Brown) Father and son went on a fishing trip. They went with a small boat with an outboard engine. The fog was coming in, the water was start getting rough and it started pouring rain the whole day.

(Wayne Brown) “And it is impossible to work in this condition during the night until we fix the problem tomorrow morning. Just send out a navigational warning. Over.”

(Wayne Brown) On the radio I started listening to the conversation and I talked with NSRI and help to assist them with the location where the guys got missing.

(Erin) Did they say hearing the fog horn and seeing the lighthouse, or even just a glimmer of it, kept them hopeful?

(Wayne Brown) Yes, because they can hear the sound of the fog horn, but they can't see the light because it was foggy weather, pouring rain, rough seas, and you know the swells are very high. So they just heard the fog horn far, far, and this was their little hope for them.

(Erin) The sound of the foghorn was a constant reminder that land was near. Wayne kept watch, and after three long days, father and son finally made it back to shore.

(Wayne Brown) That was one of my highlights. Just to save that people.

(Erin) This stretch of coastline is notorious for submerged rocks and reefs that have claimed countless ships - among them the Columbine, which sank here in 1829. Despite the threat to ships, it would take nearly a hundred years before a lighthouse was finally commissioned.

(Erin) You can imagine the relief when Cape Columbine Lighthouse was finally built – after a number of ships were lost to these waters. Since then, it’s stood here like a steadfast guardian, watching over one of the Cape’s unpredictable coastlines.

(Wayne Brown) SUBTITLES: Let’s go and sit outside. It’s a pleasant morning - lovely light mist.

(Erin) Wayne and his wife Elizabeth, have come to cherish the peace of their isolation.

(Wayne Brown) SUBTITLES: Just a light covering of mist over the water. Look there!
It’s lovely to wake up in the mornings and behold God’s gift. It’s beautiful.

(Erin) Wayne is one of a unique group committed to guiding sailors through dangerous waters.
It’s part of a living legacy, where each lighthouse is known for its unique color, shape, and the rhythm of its beam.

(Wayne Brown) You will see here, this is the lens. Our lighthouse flashes once every 15 seconds. Each lighthouse has a different flash at night. That’s how the ship identify the light at night by its flash.

(Erin) And this is all glass?

(Wayne Brown) Special molded glass. And this glass magnify the light. If you measure it in candlepower it’s about 5-million and 40-thousand candlepower. That’s how strong the light is.

(Erin) And do you come up here at night?

(Wayne Brown) Sometimes I have to do maintenance here if the light is out. I have to come and check if the light is out. What is the reason why the light is out?
(Erin) The lighthouse moves to a rhythm all its own.
Polishing the brass is just one small ritual in its care, a simple task that helps keep the great machine alive and gleaming.

(Wayne Brown) I love my work. Just the passion of it, just to see that the light is on. For me it's a big thing. That’s why I love my job.

(Erin) Along our 3,000 kilometer coastline, Cape Columbine stands as one of the few remaining lighthouses still tended by dedicated keepers. Most others are now visited only periodically by technicians.

(Erin) Wayne, what happens when you retire?

(Wayne Brown) Oh, when I’m retiring the lighthouse will be automated. There will be nobody to watch over the lighthouse. The technician is coming twice a week just to do the maintenance, but it won’t look like this. It will be overgrown because there is nobody here that actually come hands-on with the lighthouse and it's a sad thing because lighthouse keepers, they won’t employ any lighthouse keepers any more.

(Erin) It’s a rare way of life — quietly fading with the last of its keepers.
When Wayne’s watch comes to an end, so too will an era — a life of guiding lights and quiet nights, forever bound to the ocean.

VO On the rugged western Cape coast, one man keeps the lantern burning.

Wayne Brown: The lighthouse is there to guide them. But for me the best thing is when people went to sea safe and came safe back.

_______________________________________________________________________________________________

Promo 2: 21 seconds
VO He’s spent half his lifetime fulfilling an ancient duty.

Wayne Brown: For me, it's the calling and I can say it’s a life-purpose also. Because if you don't have the lighthouse here, what would happen to the big vessels and to the small boats?

VO When his watch ends, so too will an era of lighthouse keepers.

(Erin) And do you come up here at night? (Wayne Brown) Sometimes I have to do maintenance here if the light is out. I have to come and check if the light is out. What is the reason why the light is out? (Erin) The lighthouse moves to a rhythm all its own. Polishing the brass is just one small ritual in its care, a simple task that helps keep the great machine alive and gleaming. (Wayne Brown) I love my work. Just the passion of it, just to see that the light is on. For me it's a big thing. That’s why I love my job. (Erin) Along our 3,000 kilometer coastline, Cape Columbine stands as one of the few remaining lighthouses still tended by dedicated keepers. Most others are now visited only periodically by technicians. (Erin) Wayne, what happens when you retire? (Wayne Brown) Oh, when I’m retiring the lighthouse will be automated. There will be nobody to watch over the lighthouse. The technician is coming twice a week just to do the maintenance, but it won’t look like this. It will be overgrown because there is nobody here that actually come hands-on with the lighthouse and it's a sad thing because lighthouse keepers, they won’t employ any lighthouse keepers any more. (Erin) It’s a rare way of life — quietly fading with the last of its keepers. When Wayne’s watch comes to an end, so too will an era — a life of guiding lights and quiet nights, forever bound to the ocean. _________________________________________________________________________________________________ Promo 1: 21 seconds VO On the rugged western Cape coast, one man keeps the lantern burning. Wayne Brown: The lighthouse is there to guide them. But for me the best thing is when people went to sea safe and came safe back. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): On a rugged stretch of the West Coast, one man keeps the lantern burning. We follow the story of one of South Africa's final lighthouse keepers - as he keeps watch over the sea that has shaped his lif
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Lighthouses stand as timeless symbols of hope, safety, and endurance - their beams cutting through the fog and darkness to guide sailors home. But behind every shining light once stood a keeper: a quiet guardian who ensured the flame never went out.
metadata.Summary: OVERVIEW Amid crashing waves and coastal winds, Cape Columbine Lighthouse stands as a steadfast beacon. At 52, Wayne Brown has spent most of his life fulfilling that duty. Born in Paternoster and raised within sight of the tower, Wayne’s bond with the ocean runs deep. His grandfather captained a crayfish vessel; his parents worked on the lighthouse reserve. Mentored by veteran keeper Japie Greeff, Wayne inherited both the tools and the calling to keep the light burning, no matter the weather. Cape Columbine, built in 1936 and named after a ship wrecked nearby in 1829, remains one of the last manned lighthouses on South Africa’s 3,000-kilometre coastline. Most others have been automated — visited only occasionally by technicians. Yet Wayne remains, faithfully tending the beam that still cuts through fog and darkness to guide sailors safely home. “Every time a ship passes,” he says, “I know I’ve helped it find safe passage.” STORY OUTLINE ACT 1 — INTRODUCTION We open on a windswept coastline at dawn. Waves crash against the rocks as the revolving light fades into morning. A single figure walks the narrow path to the tower — Wayne Brown. Through reflective narration and natural sound, we meet the man behind the beam: a custodian of history, solitude, and purpose. ACT 2 — A LIFE BY THE SEA Through interviews and observational sequences, we trace Wayne’s life story — his childhood in the reserve, the mentorship of Japie Greeff, and the rhythm of his days at Cape Columbine. The film captures his maintenance routines, logbook entries, and quiet rituals that keep the lighthouse alive. ACT 3 — KEEPING THE LIGHT ALIVE As automation spreads, Wayne reflects on being among the last of his kind. The tone becomes more introspective: what does it mean to dedicate your life to a duty few now understand? Wayne’s voice anchors the narrative, culminating in his poetic reflection: “Die vuurtoring is ‘n lig vir die mense wat op die see is... Jy moet liefde hê vir die werk. Jy moet alles kan insit.” (The lighthouse is a light for those at sea — to show them where the safe path lies. You must have love for the work. You must give it your all.) The story closes at dusk — the light once again sweeping over the waves, a quiet testament to endurance. THEMES Tradition vs. Technology – A human craft fading in the digital age. Solitude and Purpose – Finding meaning in isolation and service. Legacy and Heritage – Preserving South Africa’s maritime past. Faith and Devotion – The lighthouse as both a beacon and a metaphor for steadfastness. TONE & VISUAL STYLE The tone is contemplative, poetic, and authentic — rooted in natural sound, minimal narration, and strong visual storytelling. Visual Style: Cinematic, slow-paced camera movement with emphasis on texture and light. A restrained colour palette of muted blues, whites, and greys, reflecting the Atlantic coast’s timeless quality. Wide aerials juxtaposed with intimate close-ups of Wayne’s hands, the turning lens, and salt-worn metal. Use of archival photographs and soundscapes (waves, gulls, foghorn) to evoke continuity and nostalgia. Key Visual Sequences: The revolving lantern at dusk and dawn. Wayne performing routine maintenance. The foghorn echoing across the sea. Archival stills of lighthouses on the South African coastline. Expansive views of the Cape Columbine Nature Reserve. WHY THIS STORY MATTERS The Lighthouse Keeper is a tribute to the quiet guardians who have watched over South Africa’s shores for generations. As automation replaces human presence, Wayne’s story preserves a piece of national heritage — reminding us that some lights still need a human touch. This is not just a story about a lighthouse. It is about duty, legacy, and devotion — a deeply human story told through the lens of one man’s enduring relationship with the sea. DELIVERABLES Broadcast-ready short documentary insert (8–10 minutes) Supporting stills of some of the lighthouses on the South African coastline ______________________________________________________________________________________________
